title: Relationships Don't Change Behavior.
author: Chris O'Brien
source: Chris O'Brien on school leadership (chrisobrienedu.substack.com), September 7, 2026
summary: In the third piece of a series, a school-leadership writer argues that the widely-used relational approach to student behavior -- build trust, and behavior will follow -- is necessary but insufficient, functioning only as a 'floor' rather than an actual intervention for a child who is struggling. Leaning heavily on Ross Greene's framework ('kids do well if they can, not if they want to'), the piece contends that schools treat a reading deficit as a skill gap to be diagnosed and taught in sequence, but treat an identical logical case -- a behavioral deficit -- as a character or relational failure, purely because a skipped word looks like 'can't' while a flipped desk looks like 'won't.' It lays out a concrete instructional method for teaching missing self-regulation skills (naming, modeling, monitoring, in ninety-second increments) and pairs it with Dr. Becky Kennedy's 'two things are true' stance, which holds that a child can be having a genuinely hard time while the behavioral expectation still stands unmoved. The piece's central structural argument is that this work cannot be left to individual classroom teachers improvising relationship-building; it requires specialist diagnosis of which specific skill is missing, and consistency across every adult a child encounters in a building, which makes it a principal's design problem rather than a teacher's interpersonal one.
points: The reading-versus-behavior thought experiment is the essay's sharpest move: the same 'kid can't yet do X' logic that triggers precise, sequenced skill instruction for a struggling reader gets replaced by vague relational questions the moment the deficit shows up as behavior instead of decoding.

Ross Greene's three lagging-skill domains (flexibility/adaptability, frustration tolerance, problem solving) are treated as teachable content with the same rigor as academic skills -- named explicitly, modeled aloud by adults, and practiced in short, repeated 90-second increments rather than one-off lessons.

Dr. Becky Kennedy's 'two things are true' stance -- a child is genuinely struggling AND the expectation still holds -- is presented as the psychological move that prevents 'he can't yet' from sliding into 'so lower the bar,' since a fixed target is what makes the skill practicable at all.

The piece explicitly reclassifies this from a teaching problem to a leadership/systems problem: a skill taught in one room and abandoned in six others isn't being taught at all, so consistency across a building's adults is a principal's design responsibility, not an individual teacher's relational skill.
quotes: Behavior is the only domain of human performance where we treat a missing skill as a question of character, and the only reason is that a reading deficit looks like inability while a behavior deficit looks like refusal. One reads as can't. The other reads as won't.
You teach it. Name the skill out loud, define it in words a child can use. Not "make better choices," which names nothing.

You do not solve a problem in the middle of the meltdown. You solve it Thursday morning when everyone is calm, about a problem you can already predict. His structure for that conversation has three steps: Empathy, Defining the adult concern, and Invitation.
He is genuinely having a hard time. And the expectation still holds. She calls the person who can hold both a sturdy leader.
You cannot practice hitting something that relocates every time you swing, and a child cannot internalize an expectation that renegotiates itself according to his mood.
A skill taught in one room for forty-seven minutes and abandoned in the other six is not being taught. It's being mentioned.
